Swift
swĭft
adj. (moving with speed; quick; rendering Hebrew qal, mahar, Greek tachus)
From Saxon swift, quick. Scripture never treats speed as a virtue in itself: it commands swiftness in hearing, denies that the race is to the swift, and warns that God Himself will be a swift witness.

Biblical Definition

Swift means quick in motion, and Scripture assigns the quality with care. It is commanded in exactly one direction, and deliberately balanced against two slownesses: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” (James 1:19). The ordering is the point. Where speed governs speech and temper instead of hearing, the proportions are simply reversed. Speed is also denied its usual advantage: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11). The Preacher is not denying that swiftness helps in a race; he is denying that the swift may count on the outcome, which providence governs. Amos presses the same denial into judgment, where the fastest man discovers that speed will not carry him out: “Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself” (Amos 2:14). And Malachi puts the adjective where it is most sobering, on God as witness: “I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless” (Malachi 3:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Moving with great speed or velocity; fleet; rapid; ready. Scripture commands men to be swift to hear and slow to speak, denies that the race is to the swift, and warns that the LORD will be a swift witness against particular sins.

expand to see more

SWIFT, a. [Sax. swift.] Moving a great distance or over a large space in a short time; moving with celerity or velocity; fleet; rapid; quick; speedy.

2. Ready; prompt; as, swift to hear.

3. Of short continuance; passing quickly; as, swift destruction.

SWIFT, n. The current of a stream; also, a bird of the swallow kind, remarkable for its rapid flight.

SWIFTLY, adv. With celerity or velocity; fleetly; rapidly; with quick motion.

SWIFTNESS, n. Speed; rapid motion; quickness; celerity; velocity; rapidity.

Key Scripture

James 1:19 — "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:"

Ecclesiastes 9:11 — "I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all."

Amos 2:14 — "Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself:"

Malachi 3:5 — "And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

James's proportions have been inverted by an age built for instant reply: men are swift to speak and swift to wrath, and the one swiftness commanded — hearing — is the one now least practised.

expand to see more

James 1:19 reads as a direct description of modern discourse with every term reversed. The instruments men now use for speech are designed for immediate response and reward the quickest and most heated reply, which means the ordinary conditions of life train the two slownesses out of a man while making speed of speech and of anger effortless. The verse is not a counsel of passivity. Swiftness is commanded — toward hearing — and hearing in James means the receiving of the engrafted word and the doing of it. A generation swift in the two forbidden directions and slow in the commanded one has exactly inverted the Apostle's order.

The second corruption is confidence in speed itself, and Ecclesiastes 9:11 addresses it without cynicism. The Preacher grants that swiftness, strength, wisdom, and skill are real advantages; he denies that they secure the result, because time and chance — which the believer knows as providence — happen to them all. That is a rebuke to the man who trusts his own quickness and a comfort to the man who has none. Malachi 3:5 completes the picture by putting the adjective where it belongs at last: the LORD is the swift one, and He is swift as a witness against the very oppressions that fast and clever men commit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qal (light, swift) and mahar (to hasten) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek tachus (quick, swift) is the adjective of James 1:19.

expand to see more

Hebrew qal (H7031) — light, swift; used of swift runners and of the swift of foot in Amos 2:14.

Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, to be swift; the verb behind the LORD's swift witness in Malachi 3:5.

Hebrew merowts (H4793) — a running, a race; the race that is not to the swift in Ecclesiastes 9:11.

Greek tachus (G5036) — quick, swift, ready; the adjective governing “swift to hear”.

Greek bradus (G1021) — slow, dull; the counterpart commanded toward speech and wrath.

Usage

"“Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath” — speed is commanded in one direction only."

"“The race is not to the swift” — advantage is real; the outcome is providence's."

"“I will be a swift witness” — the swiftness that finally matters is God's."
